title: Thread Communication
summary: Thread communication in Java: how wait, notify, and BlockingQueue coordinate producer-consumer handoff without polling, and where hand-rolled signaling breaks.

refs.title: What is Thread? Low-power IoT Networking for Smart Home Devices
Thread Communication - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **Thread communication is not threads talking. It is threads agreeing on state under one lock.** One thread changes a predicate like `queue not empty`, then wakes a thread parked on the *same* monitor. If you signal without holding the lock, wait on a different object, or check the condition without a loop, you have no communication — you have a race.

In Java, inter-thread communication means **ordered handoff of shared state between threads without busy-spinning**. The low-level form is `Object.wait()`, `notify()`, and `notifyAll()`, called only while holding the monitor of that same object via `synchronized`. `wait()` atomically releases the lock and parks the thread. `notify()` or `notifyAll()` moves one or all parked threads back to runnable, but does not release the lock — the woken thread still has to re-acquire it before it runs again. The higher-level form is `java.util.concurrent`: `BlockingQueue`, `Condition`, `Semaphore`, `CountDownLatch`, which wrap the exact same park-and-wake pattern so you do not hand-roll it. Either way the goal is identical: do not burn CPU checking `while(queue.isEmpty()) {}`, park instead and let the state changer wake you.

Separate three jobs that candidates blur together. **Mutual exclusion** means only one thread mutates the buffer at a time — that is `synchronized` or `Lock`. **Visibility** means a write by thread A is observable by thread B — that is the happens-before edge created by unlocking and re-locking the same monitor, or by a concurrent collection. **Ordering** means B does not proceed until a predicate is true, like *buffer non-empty* or *buffer not full* — that is `wait()` plus a re-check loop. `volatile` gives you visibility but no ordering. `synchronized` alone gives you exclusion and visibility but no efficient ordering. `wait` / `notify` exists only for the third job, and it only works because it temporarily gives up the first job while preserving the second.
The mechanism: monitor, wait set, and re-check

Every Java object can act as a monitor: an entry set of threads blocked trying to enter `synchronized`, plus a wait set of threads that called `wait()` and gave up the lock. The reason `wait()` must own the lock is atomicity — the check-then-park sequence has to be indivisible, otherwise the signal lands between your `if(empty)` test and your park, and you sleep forever. That is why the JVM throws `IllegalMonitorStateException` if you call `wait()` or `notify()` outside `synchronized(obj)`. The reason you re-check in `while`, not `if`, is that wakeup is not a guarantee: spurious wakeups exist, `notifyAll()` wakes threads whose predicate may still be false, and multiple consumers can race so only the first one to re-acquire the lock finds work. The loop turns *I was woken* into *the condition I need is actually true now*.

blocks.title: Wait and notify lifecycle
blocks.caption: Producer and consumer contend for the same monitor; wait releases it, notifyAll re-arms contention.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  P1["Producer enters synchronized queue"] --> P2{"queue full?"}
  P2 -- Yes --> P3["queue wait: release lock and park"]
  P2 -- No --> P4["add item and notifyAll"]
  P4 --> P5["exit synchronized: release lock"]
  P5 --> P1
  P3 --> P1
  C1["Consumer enters synchronized queue"] --> C2{"queue empty?"}
  C2 -- Yes --> C3["queue wait: release lock and park"]
  C2 -- No --> C4["remove item and notifyAll"]
  C4 --> C5["exit synchronized: release lock"]
  C5 --> C1
  C3 --> C1

blocks.text: Read the diagram literally. The producer and consumer never signal each other directly — they signal *through the buffer state*. Producer adds, then calls `notifyAll()` while still holding the lock; that only moves consumers from the wait set to the entry set. The actual handoff happens when the producer exits `synchronized` and the OS reschedules a consumer to re-acquire the lock and re-test `while(queue.isEmpty())`. That is why `notify()` does not mean *hand over the lock now*. It means *re-check soon*. Choose `notifyAll()` by default when you have more than one waiter type or more than one consumer, because `notify()` can wake a producer when only a consumer can make progress — a textbook missed-signal deadlock. You pay one thundering-herd re-check to buy correctness. That trade-off is almost always worth it for a bounded buffer.

blocks.caption: Pick by predicate complexity and number of waiter types, not by fashion.
rows: `wait + notify`
Manual predicate + single monitor, one waiter woken
Zero dependencies, exact control over custom condition; good for interview baseline
You own every bug: missed signal, wrong monitor, `if` instead of `while`, `notify` starvation
`wait + notifyAll`
Manual predicate + single monitor, all waiters woken
Correct default for multiple producers and consumers; survives heterogeneous waiters
Wakes threads that re-check and re-park; wasted context switches under high contention
`Lock + Condition`
`await` / `signal` / `signalAll` with separate condition queues
Two conditions (`notFull`, `notEmpty`) so you wake only the useful side; interruptible and timed waits
More code, must `unlock` in `finally`; still manual predicate logic
`BlockingQueue`
Encapsulated `put` / `take` that block internally
No explicit wait, no missed signal, no monitor bookkeeping; the production answer
Fixed queue semantics; cannot express arbitrary predicates like *wait until two slots free*
`Semaphore / CountDownLatch / Exchanger`
Permits, one-shot gate, or pairwise rendezvous
Clean for startup gates, rate limits, one-shot sequencing without a buffer
Not a buffer; forcing data transfer through a latch produces convoluted state

blocks.text: My opinion is blunt: **never hand-roll `wait` / `notify` in production unless the predicate cannot be expressed as queue-full or queue-empty.** `BlockingQueue` was chosen precisely to collapse exclusion, visibility, and ordering into `put()` and `take()`. You trade a small loss of expressiveness for the elimination of four failure modes you will otherwise ship. `Lock` plus two `Condition` objects is the middle ground I accept when you need *wake producers only* versus *wake consumers only* and can prove the contention justifies it. Raw `notify()` instead of `notifyAll()` is almost never the right optimisation — the one context switch you save is not worth the liveness proof you now owe every reviewer.
How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Broken thread communication rarely throws. It stalls, duplicates work, or corrupts the buffer under load — exactly when you cannot attach a debugger. Learn the mapping from root cause to observable symptom so you can diagnose from thread dumps and metrics instead of guessing.

items: **Missed signal: thread parks after the state already changed.** Cause: check-then-wait without holding the lock across both, or waiting on object A while notifying on object B. Symptom: consumer stuck in `WAITING` on `Object.wait` forever while the queue sits non-empty; producer idle. In a dump you see one parked consumer, zero lock contention, throughput drops to zero.

**`if` instead of `while`: woken thread proceeds on a false predicate.** Cause: spurious wakeup, `notifyAll` waking every waiter, or two consumers racing so the loser finds the queue empty again. Symptom: `NoSuchElementException`, `NullPointerException` on poll, or negative size accounting that only reproduces under parallel load. Intermittent, never in a single-threaded test.

**`notify` starvation with mixed waiters.** Cause: multiple producers and consumers but `notify()` wakes same-type thread — producer wakes producer when the queue is still full. Symptom: system freezes with a full queue and parked consumers that were never woken. Switching to `notifyAll()` or splitting into `notFull` / `notEmpty` conditions makes it vanish, which is your confirmation.

**`IllegalMonitorStateException` on `wait` / `notify`.** Cause: calling either outside `synchronized` on the same object, or synchronising on `this` but waiting on the queue field. Symptom: loud, immediate crash on first concurrent path. It is the only failure that is easy — treat it as a design smell that your monitor object is ambiguous. Fix by synchronising on a private final lock object and never `this`.

**Lock held across `notify` plus slow work, or `notify` never reached.** Cause: doing I/O, logging, or long computation while still inside `synchronized` after `notifyAll`, or an exception before the `notify` line. Symptom: latency spikes and `BLOCKED` threads piled on the monitor in dumps; woken threads cannot re-acquire. Fix by mutating state, signalling, and exiting the critical section fast — never call back out to unknown code while holding the monitor.

blocks.title: The three-line contract
blocks.text: **Same monitor. `while`, not `if`. `notifyAll` by default.** Wait in `while(!predicate) lock.wait()`, mutate state, then `lock.notifyAll()` before leaving `synchronized`. Violate any one and the code may pass ten demos and deadlock on the eleventh run.
Code that proves you understand it

Write the hand-rolled version first in an interview to prove you know the monitor rules, then say you would ship the second version. The difference in line count is the argument for `BlockingQueue`: every line you delete is a race you no longer have to prove absent. Note why the first version synchronises on the queue itself, re-checks capacity in a loop, and notifies *after* mutation.

items.title: Implement a bounded producer-consumer
items.text: Expect a fixed-capacity buffer with blocking `put` and `take`. Start by naming the monitor, the predicate for each side, and the lock scope — then write the `while + wait + notifyAll` version. They grade monitor choice and loop structure before correctness of the happy path.

items.title: Add N producers and M consumers
items.text: The follow-up that kills `notify()` and `if`. Explain why one producer must be able to wake any of several consumers, why losers of the re-acquire race must re-park, and why shared-prefix state like size must only be touched under the lock. Switch to `notifyAll()` and defend the extra wakeups as a liveness tax.

items.title: Diagnose a deadlock or lost wakeup
items.text: You will be shown code that waits on one object and notifies on another, or checks `if(empty)` once. Walk the interleaving out loud: signal lands before park, thread sleeps forever. Point at the thread-dump signature — `WAITING` with no contention versus `BLOCKED` pile-up — to show production fluency.

items.title: Handle spurious wakeups and interrupts
items.text: Say the JVM permits `wait()` to return without a `notify`, so the loop is mandatory, not defensive. Propagate `InterruptedException` or restore the interrupt flag; swallowing it strands worker shutdown. Offer a timed `wait(timeout)` variant only if they ask for backpressure with deadlines.

items.title: Modernise it to production code
items.text: Close by replacing the whole monitor with `ArrayBlockingQueue` or `LinkedBlockingQueue`, or `Lock` with `notFull` / `notEmpty` conditions if they demand selective wakeup. Name the trade-off: you lose custom predicates but delete missed-signal and wrong-monitor bugs entirely. That sentence is what separates a Medium pass from a Strong Hire.

items: **`notify()` hands the lock to the waiter.** It does not. It only moves a thread from the wait set to the entry set. The lock transfers at the next `synchronized` exit. Code that assumes immediate handoff and keeps mutating state after `notify()` corrupts the predicate the waiter is about to re-check.

**Polling with `sleep()` is simpler and fine.** It trades correctness bugs for permanent costs: latency bounded by sleep interval plus wasted CPU and noisy wakeups. `wait()` parks with zero CPU until the state actually changes. Polling is only acceptable when the condition source lives outside the JVM and cannot signal you.

**`volatile` or `ConcurrentHashMap` replaces `wait` / `notify`.** They solve visibility, not ordering. A consumer spinning on a `volatile boolean ready` still busy-waits; a map gives you safe publication but no blocking take. You need either a blocking primitive or an explicit wait set to park efficiently.

**`notifyAll()` is always wasteful; prefer `notify()`.** `notify()` is an optimisation that requires proving only one waiter type exists and only one waiter can make progress. With producers *and* consumers parked, that proof usually fails. Default to `notifyAll()`; reach for `notify()` or split `Condition`s only with measured contention to justify it.

**`wait()` can be called on any object from anywhere.** It must be the exact object you synchronised on, inside that critical section. Waiting on a field while locking `this`, or locking a freshly assigned lock reference, silently creates two monitors and guarantees missed signals. Use a `private final Object lock` and never reassign it.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Hand-rolled signaling is a teaching tool and an escape hatch, not a default.
rows: Bounded buffer with blocking put and take
Use `BlockingQueue`
Encapsulates monitor, predicate, and re-check; no missed-signal surface
Custom predicate, e.g. wait until batch of K items or two resources free
Hand-roll `wait + notifyAll` or `Lock + Condition`
Queue semantics cannot express it; you need an explicit wait set and loop
One-shot startup gate: workers wait until initialisation done
Use `CountDownLatch`
Single transition needs no buffer; latch gives happens-before without a monitor loop
Permit pool or rate limiter
Use `Semaphore`
Counting permits maps directly; hand-rolled counters reintroduce lost-wakeup bugs
High-throughput pipeline with backpressure and metrics
Use `BlockingQueue` or reactive channel, never polling
Polling adds latency and CPU at exactly the load where you can afford neither

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: "Threads coordinate by mutating guarded state under one monitor and parking in `while(!condition) lock.wait()` until the mutator calls `notifyAll()` — and in production I would ship that as a `BlockingQueue` unless the predicate needs custom conditions."
